d: Light sources simulate realistic lighting from objects such as torches, spotlights, and screens.
h:
Local light sources simulate realistic lighting from objects such as lamps, torches, spotlights, and TV screens. By using the different types of light sources instead of just general global lighting through the Lighting service, you can create immersive environments such as cyberpunk cities, traditional light festivals, and moody detective scenes.

The LightingStyle property, modifiable only in the Properties window for the global Lighting object, sets your game's lighting style. For more information, see Appearance.

To view light guides that indicate the color and field of effect from light sources, such as the angle of light emission from the cone's apex of a SpotLight, open Studio Settings and toggle on Show Light Guides.

Light types

Local light sources include PointLight, SpotLight, and SurfaceLight. Each shares various properties from the Light class, including Color, Brightness, and Shadows.

PointLight

A PointLight emits light spherically from a single point. This object is ideal for non-directional lights like bulbs, torches, and fireballs.

To create a point light in Studio, insert a PointLight into an Attachment or a BasePart (Attachment is recommended for point‑specific light emission). Then adjust the object's Range as well as shared properties like Brightness and Color.

Range

A point light's Range property defines the radial distance of illumination from the light's position, measured in studs.

SpotLight

A SpotLight emits light in the shape of a cone with a spherical base. This object is ideal for directional lights like street lamps, flashlights, and headlights.

To create a spotlight in Studio, insert a SpotLight into an Attachment or a BasePart and set its Face property to specify which direction light emits from. Then adjust the Angle and Range, as well as shared properties like Brightness and Color.

Face

A spotlight's Face property determines which face/axis light emits from, as shown from the following streetlamp's glowing light part:

Angle

A spotlight's Angle property defines the angle of light emission from the cone's apex. The maximum value is 180 which illuminates a full half sphere from the apex.

SurfaceLight

A SurfaceLight emits light from the face of a BasePart. This object is ideal for lighting from computer screens, billboards, signs, and fluorescent panels.

To create a surface light in Studio, insert a SurfaceLight into a BasePart and set its Face property to specify which surface light emits from. Then adjust the Angle and Range, as well as shared properties like Brightness and Color.

Face

A surface light's Face property determines the face of the BasePart from which light emanates. Notice that light emits from the entire surface, not just a point on the surface.

Angle

A surface light's Angle property defines the angle of light emission from the part's surface. An angle of 0 means that light travels directly outward from the surface while an angle of 180 means light travels outward perpendicular to the surface.

Shared properties

All light sources share various properties from the Light class, including color, brightness, and shadows.

Color

The Color property sets the Color3 value of the emitted light.

Brightness

The Brightness property sets the light's brightness with maximum effect at the center of the light. Note that Brightness is still limited to the light's defined range, so a higher Brightness value doesn't light up a larger region around the light.

Shadows

The Shadows property projects shadows where light is blocked by an obstacle.

kid.simple: This page explains the three kinds of lights you can put on objects: point lights, spotlights, and surface lights. These local lights glow from a specific object, unlike the overall sky lighting. They let you build cozy torch-lit caves, neon cities, or spooky flashlight scenes. You can set each light's color, brightness, range, and shadows.
kid.analogy: It is like lighting a room for a play: a bare bulb lights everything around it, a flashlight only lights where it points, and a glowing TV screen lights up whatever is in front of it.
keyPoints: `PointLight` glows equally in all directions from one point. Use it for bulbs, torches, and fireballs.
`SpotLight` shines in a cone. Use it for street lamps, flashlights, and headlights. `Angle` controls how wide the cone is, up to 180 (a full half-sphere).
`SurfaceLight` glows from a whole face of a part. Use it for screens, signs, and light panels.
`Face` on spotlights and surface lights picks which side of the part the light comes out of.
`Range` is how far the light reaches, in studs. A range of 12 lights up things up to 12 studs away.
All lights share `Color`, `Brightness`, and `Shadows`. Brightness is strongest at the center but never reaches farther than the range.
To insert a light, add it into an Attachment or a part in the Explorer. Attachments are best for a light from one exact spot.
Turn on Show Light Guides in Studio Settings to see where each light reaches.

terms.local light: A light that comes from a specific object, as opposed to global lighting from the `Lighting` service that lights the whole world.
terms.range: How far, in studs, the light reaches from its source. Outside that distance it adds no light at all.
terms.brightness: How strong the light is near its center. Turning brightness from 2 to 10 makes the lit area brighter, not bigger.
terms.cone: An ice-cream-cone shape. Spotlights shine out in this shape from their tip.
terms.apex: The pointed tip of the cone, where the spotlight's light starts.
terms.angle: How wide the light spreads. A spotlight with Angle 30 is a narrow beam; 75 is much wider.
terms.Color3: A color made of red, green, and blue numbers. [255, 100, 50] is an orange.
terms.shadows: Dark areas where an object blocks the light. Turning `Shadows` on makes blocked areas dark.
terms.Face: One side of a part, like Top, Bottom, Left, Right, Front, or Back.

example.title: Add an orange torch glow to a part
example.place: Script inside a Part in Workspace
example.code:
local part = script.Parent

local light = Instance.new("PointLight")
light.Color = Color3.fromRGB(255, 100, 50) -- warm orange
light.Brightness = 2
light.Range = 12 -- lights things up to 12 studs away
light.Shadows = true
light.Parent = part

-- Make it flicker like a real flame
while true do
	light.Brightness = 1.5 + math.random() -- between 1.5 and 2.5
	task.wait(0.1)
end
explain: We create a `PointLight` so it glows in every direction.
`Range = 12` means the light reaches 12 studs from the part.
Putting the light inside the part makes it glow from there.
The loop changes the brightness a little every 0.1 seconds, so it flickers like fire.

watchOut: Raising `Brightness` will not make a light reach farther. Raise `Range` for that.
A spotlight pointing the wrong way usually has the wrong `Face`. Change `Face` or rotate the part.
Lots of lights with shadows on can slow down weaker devices. Use only what you need.
